conventions: Each value carries source_url and a supporting quote or stated locator. 'read_from_figure' means taken off a plotted graph by eye, with lower precision. 'computed' means arithmetic done here from cited values, never a published figure. Values not actually read at a source are listed in not_read, without a number.

smartbird.subject: Festo SmartBird, herring gull inspired flapping-wing model with active torsion

primary_source.citation: Send W, Fischer M, Jebens K, Mugrauer R, Nagarathinam A, Scharstein F. Artificial Hinged-Wing Bird with Active Torsion and Partially Linear Kinematics. 28th Congress of the International Council of the Aeronautical Sciences (ICAS 2012), paper 053.
primary_source.note: M. Fischer is listed as Festo GmbH & Co. KG and R. Mugrauer as Effekt-Technik GmbH. The task named 'Send et al. 2012'; this is that paper, read in full.

design_point.quote: Operational data at design point: Speed 5 m/s, flapping frequency 2 Hz, average energy consumption 23 W.

measured_free_flight.quote: The average velocity was determined to be u0 = 4.7 m/s ... The net power is obtained from the total power of Pel = 18 W by subtracting the bias power of the servo motors, which is measured during passive flight and amounts to P0,sv = 5 W.
measured_free_flight.locator: Section 3.4; Fig. 8 caption gives 'a typical horizontal flight (18 W)'

net_flapping_power_w.quote: The net power of Pel - P0,sv = 13 W

climb_power_peak_w.locator: Fig. 8, climbing trace, about 42 W peak settling to about 25-32 W

v4_power_targets.flag_for_orchestrator: SPEC V4 says 'the published figure', but the primary paper publishes two: 23 W at the 5 m/s design point and 18 W measured in horizontal free flight at 4.7 m/s. Each must be compared at its own speed. The +/-30% band differs: 16.1-29.9 W on 23 W, 12.6-23.4 W on 18 W. This should be declared before V4 runs. Secondary sources repeat only 23 W.

span_m.disagreement: 2 m in the primary paper, 6.5 ft (1.98 m) in Machine Design, 6 ft in ZME Science. A Festo figure of 1.96 m is widely reported but Festo's pages could not be read directly; see not_read.

mass_kg.disagreement: Use 0.48 kg with the battery from the primary paper. A Festo figure of 450 g is widely reported but Festo's pages could not be read directly; see not_read.

wing_section.text: Fig. 12 compares SmartBird's wing section with NACA7412 'applied during the design process'. Coordinates of the actual section are not given.

structure.text: Two-part inner wing spar, trapezoidal hinge, outer wing spar. Inner wing generates lift, outer wing generates thrust; both spars torsionally stiff. Lagging degree of freedom not implemented.

values.locator: Fig. 2B screenshot label '1.96 Hz', on the wing position trace during flight

reduced_frequency.definition: omega* = omega c / 2 / u0, with c the mean chord 0.25 m

transmission.quote: a two-stage spur gearing with a 1:45 reduction of speed
transmission.hinge_ratio_quote: Via the trapezoidal hinge, a 1:3 transmission ratio is achieved.
transmission.disagreement: Machine Design calls the same 1:45 drive 'a two-stage helical transmission'.

stroke_2d_section.locator: Fig. 2A, z(t) = -h(t) on the right axis, peak near +/-0.3 m, described as 'typical amplitudes'
stroke_2d_section.limitation: This is a typical 2D section plunge, not a stated full-wing stroke. The paper gives no flap stroke angle in degrees and says wing torsion and bending in free flight 'remain still unknown'.

torsion.locator: Fig. 2A, alpha(t) plateau near +/-9 deg, with the turn inside the 60-120 deg and 240-300 deg phase windows
torsion.shape: Partially linear: the outer wing holds a constant angle, then turns within a short part of the period around the plunge extremes.
torsion.quote: When the wings flap upwards, the servomotor for the active torsion turns the outer wing from a positive angle of incidence within a short fraction of the flapping period into a negative angle of incidence. Between the turning points the angle of torsion remains constant.
torsion.twist_applied_at: A servomotor at the outer wing tip twists the wing against the spar through the outermost rib.

phase_shift_deg.quote_nominal: in flapping flight the phase shift of plunge is defined to be 90 deg ahead of pitch

cfd_case_parameters.definitions: lambda_c = h0 / (alpha0 c); omega_c* = omega c / u0
cfd_case_parameters.locator: Fig. 11 captions. Lambda values read from the marked square on each plot. Data 'refer to the earlier model' of Fig. 3.

thrust_n.quote: thrust force FT = eta_tot (Pel - P0,sv)/u0 = 0.7 N

cL.basis: weight 0.48 kg, rho 1.2 kg/m3, A 0.5 m2, u0 4.7 m/s

cL_over_cD.quote: cL / cD = 7 in free sustained horizontal flight

eta_total.quote: measured total efficiency eta_tot = 0.25 (Fig. 5) in tethered flight

eta_aero.quote: high values achieved for eta_aero above 0.6 and up to 0.8

values.locator: Fig. 5, eta_em trace near 0.4 on the right axis

tethered_vs_free.quote: Measurements in free flight show even lower values for the required electric power than the data during tethered flight.

sensitivity.quote: Flight tests show a very sensitive dependence of thrust generation on the torsion shape function.

internal_consistency_checks_computed.reduced_frequency_at_2_hz: 2 pi x 2 x 0.125 / 4.7 = 0.33, inside the 0.3-0.45 range
internal_consistency_checks_computed.reynolds: 4.7 x 0.25 / 1.5e-5 = 78,000, with an assumed sea-level kinematic viscosity of 1.5e-5 m2/s; matches about 80,000

not_read: Festo's SmartBird pages and brochure could not be opened: festo.com, media.festo.com/media/113631_documentation.pdf and the 2011 brochure PDF all returned HTTP 403, and web.archive.org was refused or rate limited. Search-engine excerpts attribute a span of 1.96 m, 2.00 m, a torso length of 1.07 m and a mass of about 450 g to Festo pages. These are not used as values here. A human opening media.festo.com/media/113631_documentation.pdf would close this gap.
The Engineer, Control Engineering, Time and RoboAid articles returned HTTP 403.

morphology.method_note: Alerstam et al. give mean equivalent airspeed Ue in continuous flapping flight tracked by radar, plus biometry. Their wing span is maximum wingtip to wingtip on a bird in the hand. Their wing area is the projected area of both wings fully stretched, including the body between the wings. Aspect ratio is computed here as b^2/S.

source.citation: Alerstam T, Rosen M, Backman J, Ericson PGP, Hellgren O. Flight speeds among bird species: allometric and phylogenetic effects. PLoS Biology 5(8): e197 (2007), Protocol S1.
source.licence: PLOS Biology articles are published open access under CC BY; check the article page before redistributing the table.

rock_pigeon_columba_livia.wing_area_note: The table header says only 'Wing area [cm2]' beside other single-wing quantities. It is not stated whether this is one wing or both. Do not compute aspect ratio from it without checking Van Den Berg and Rayner (1995).
rock_pigeon_columba_livia.row_verbatim: Columba livia Rock pigeon 293 B95 27.63 T08 22.47 B95 323 B95 71 B95 172.7 B95 314 B95 6.7 B95
rock_pigeon_columba_livia.source_note: eLife article 89968, Supplementary File 3a, values attributed to B95 = C. Van Den Berg and J. M. V. Rayner. The primary 1995 paper was not read.
rock_pigeon_columba_livia.cruise_speed_note: Alerstam Protocol S1 has no Columba livia row. Tobalske and Dial (1996) flew pigeons at 6-20 m/s in a wind tunnel and report that wingbeat frequency 'did not change appreciably with increasing flight speed' during steady flight, which is a test range rather than a cruise value. https://umimpact.umt.edu/en/publications/flight-kinematics-of-black-billed-magpies-and-pigeons-over-a-wide/

columba_oenas.caution: Only one span and one area measurement. Its aspect ratio looks anomalously high for the genus; use with care.

rock_pigeon_columba_livia.moment_of_inertia_note: Header extracts as '[106 kg m2]', with the exponent's sign lost in the PDF text; it is probably 1e-6 kg m2. Check the PDF before use.

pennycuick.status: Not read. C. J. Pennycuick, J. Exp. Biol. 199, 1613-1618 (1996) and 204, 3283 (2001) returned HTTP 403 at the publisher. Alerstam Protocol S1 lists Pennycuick (1999) among its biometry sources.
